## Censored support vector regression

`method = "svm"` fits a censored **regression** SVM to all training rows.
Its objective differs from ranking SVM and ordinary regression on observed times.
The default is compact `solver = "clarabel"`, a required R dependency.
There is no silent dense fallback. Explicit `solver = "quadprog"` retains
the dense reference numerical path. Explicit
`solver = "osqp"`, `solver = "clarabel"` or `solver = "newton"` uses compact
algebra for linear and additive kernels, preserving the reference's adjusted
quadratic objective. There is no automatic solver or kernel substitution.

The implementation follows the regression convention in `survivalsvm` 0.0.6,
including its `Matrix::nearPD` correction and five-decimal support coefficients.
It does not claim that this correction is a new statistical method or that it
is identical to every textbook formulation of censored SVR.

Both kernels are implemented internally. Fitting, tuning
and prediction do not require `survivalsvm` or `pracma`. `survivalsvm` is retained
only for optional independent reference tests. The dense path calls
`quadprog::solve.QP` directly, with the same objective signs and constraint order
as the reference implementation. Linear Newton uses base R optimization;
the default uses `clarabel`, OSQP uses `osqp`, the dense reference uses
`quadprog`, and compact additive fits additionally use `RSpectra`.
All of these solver packages are installed as required dependencies.
The dense solver provides a numerical reference. It can return an
infeasible iterate on ill-conditioned linear problems. Non-finite or infeasible
solutions cause an error before a model is returned.
They cannot produce predictions or win tuning. Prediction also rejects saved
engines explicitly marked as infeasible or failed. The compact solvers are
the recommended computational paths.

## The reference quadratic program

Let $X$ denote the training-standardized design, $t$ observed positive times,
$\delta$ event indicators, and $K$ the selected kernel ($XX^\top$ for linear).
Define
\[
q=(-t^\top,(\delta\odot t)^\top)^\top,\qquad
a=(-\mathbf{1}^\top,\delta^\top)^\top.
\]
The numerical reference minimizes
\[
\frac12 u^\top H u+q^\top u,
\qquad a^\top u=0,\quad 0\leq u_i\leq C,
\]
where $u$ contains $2n$ coefficients and $H$ is the positive-definite matrix
returned by `nearPD` for the block matrix assembled by the reference engine.
Its symmetrized form is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}K&-M\\-M&K\end{pmatrix},\qquad
M=\tfrac12\{\operatorname{diag}(\delta)K+
 K\operatorname{diag}(\delta)\}.
\]
Switching directly to the engine's `ipop` path is **not** an equivalent
replacement: that path does not apply the same `nearPD` correction.

## Linear structure, without a kernel approximation

Write $Z=\operatorname{diag}(\delta)X$. Both $K+M$ and $K-M$ lie in the
column span of $[X,Z]$. A thin SVD of this matrix therefore reduces the
nonzero eigensystems to at most $2p$ dimensions each. The implementation
removes only numerical SVD null directions (relative threshold $10^{-12}$),
well below the reference eigenvalue cutoff $10^{-6}$.

Let $Q\Lambda Q^\top$ be the reference's retained positive projection and
$\epsilon=10^{-8}\lambda_{\max}$. Without correlation or fixed-diagonal
constraints, the repeated positive projection in `nearPD` is unchanged.
Its final eigenvalue floor and diagonal rescaling can be written as
\[
H=S\{\epsilon I+Q(\Lambda-\epsilon I)Q^\top\}S
  =D_0+LL^\top,
\]
where $S$ is the same diagonal rescaling, $D_0=\epsilon S^2$ and
$L=SQ(\Lambda-\epsilon I)^{1/2}$. Consequently, the equivalent sparse QP is
\[
\min_{u,v}\ \frac12u^\top D_0u+\frac12v^\top v+q^\top u,
\quad v=L^\top u,\quad a^\top u=0,\quad 0\leq u\leq C.
\]
All $n$ observations still enter the objective and constraints. This is not
Nystrom, random features, or a truncated kernel approximation. Storage for
the design and Hessian factors is proportional to $np+nr$, where $r$ is the
retained rank, rather than storing the dense $2n$ by $2n$ Hessian. Solver
factorizations have additional memory costs; the package does not promise
linear runtime for arbitrary designs.

## Additive structure and the same spectral cutoff

The additive kernel in the reference, on numeric encoded columns, is
\[
K_{i\ell}=\sum_{j=1}^p\left(1-
 \frac{|x_{ij}-x_{\ell j}|}{R_j}\right),\qquad
R_j=\max_i x_{ij}-\min_i x_{ij}.
\]
For a column sorted as $t_1\le\cdots\le t_n$, let $A_i=\sum_{\ell\le i}v_\ell$
and $B_i=\sum_{\ell\le i}t_\ell v_\ell$. Then
\[
\sum_\ell |t_i-t_\ell|v_\ell
 =t_i(2A_i-A_n)-(2B_i-B_n).
\]
This identity works for signed vectors and ties. Products with $K$ require
sorted prefix sums, not an $n$ by $n$ array. Products with $K\pm M$ follow
using two products with $K$ and elementwise multiplication by $\delta$.

RSpectra computes the largest algebraic eigenvalues of these operators.
The requested count grows until the converged spectrum includes an eigenvalue
below the **reference's existing** $10^{-6}\lambda_{\max}$ cutoff. There is no
user-selected smaller rank. Residuals, the excluded boundary and the cutoff are
stored; incomplete or numerically ambiguous boundary results raise errors.
Small or nearly full-rank blocks use dense block eigendecomposition only if
the memory planning limit allows it. The same positive floor and original-row
diagonal rescaling are then applied. This is a numerical eigensolver for the
reference projection, not a claim of symbolic or bitwise arithmetic equality.

Prediction uses the same prefix identity with support coefficients. Ranges
are calculated from the **support vectors**, as in the original implementation,
not silently replaced by the full training ranges. Values outside those ranges
are evaluated by the original formula, not clipped.

## Exact multiplicities, not a training subsample

Only rows with identical encoded predictors, observed time **and** event may
share a frequency group. Let $P$ be group membership, $W=\operatorname{diag}(m_g)$
the multiplicities, and $R=PW^{-1/2}$, so $R^\top R=I$. Kernel spectra are
computed with $W^{1/2}K_gW^{1/2}$, not the unweighted representative matrix.
The full reference diagonal rescaling is recovered before restricting the QP;
applying `nearPD` naively to an unweighted reduced data set is not equivalent.

Permutation symmetry within a group, the identical linear terms, equal bounds
and strictly positive diagonal floor imply that the unique optimum has equal
coordinates within each group. With $U=\operatorname{blockdiag}(R,R)$,
the exact restriction $u=Uz$ gives
\[
\min_z\ \tfrac12z^\top U^\top HU z+(U^\top q)^\top z,
\quad (U^\top a)^\top z=0,\quad 0\le z_g\le C\sqrt{m_g}.
\]
Every original coefficient is restored as $u_i=z_{g(i)}/\sqrt{m_{g(i)}}$
**before** rounding and support selection. Thus support residual means still
count all original observations. Counts, membership and original-length dual
coefficients remain available in the fit. Set `collapse_duplicates = FALSE`
to audit without this algebraic compression. It is not censoring-dependent
subsampling, approximate deduplication, or a change of the penalty per row.

## An equivalent small dual and Newton solver

For a compact QP with $H=D_0+LL^\top$, write $d_i=(D_0)_{ii}>0$ and $b_i$
for its box bounds (including multiplicity scaling, when used). Define
\[
\psi_i(s)=\min_{0\le z_i\le b_i}
 \{\tfrac12d_i z_i^2+s z_i\},\qquad
z_i(s)=\min\{b_i,\max(0,-s/d_i)\}.
\]
The negative dual is
\[
F(\theta,\mu)=\tfrac12\|\theta\|^2-
 \sum_i\psi_i(q_i+L_i^\top\theta+\mu a_i).
\]
For each $\theta$, a monotone scalar root solve enforces $a^\top z=0$.
The remaining problem has only $r$ free coordinates, where $r$ is the number
of modes retained by the reference projection. Its gradient is
$\theta-L^\top z$. On a cell with free box coordinates $A$, its Hessian is
\[
I+L_A^\top D_A^{-1}L_A-
\frac{(L_A^\top D_A^{-1}a_A)(L_A^\top D_A^{-1}a_A)^\top}
 {a_A^\top D_A^{-1}a_A},
\]
with the last term omitted if its denominator vanishes. The value is
continuously differentiable and piecewise quadratic; this is not a claim of
global twice differentiability at box transitions.

`solver = "newton"` supplies these analytic derivatives to R's `stats::nlm`,
using `stats::uniroot` for the equality. Solver status alone is insufficient.
Box stationarity holds by construction, and an independent certificate checks
the equality and the conservative gap bound
\[
\tfrac12\|\theta-L^\top z\|^2+|\mu a^\top z|.
\]
The relative bound must not exceed `tolerance`; equality must satisfy
`max(1e-7, 10 * tolerance)`. Iteration/step-limit failures are rejected.
An `nlm` line-search stop is accepted only if the independent certificate passes;
the optimizer code is retained separately. Analytic derivatives are also
tested against finite differences away from box transitions.

## Tuning and prediction

```{r, eval=FALSE}
fit <- surv_tune(Surv(time, event) ~ temperature + age, data,
  method = "svm", grid = list(cost = c(0.01, 0.1, 1)),
  params = list(solver = "clarabel"), folds = 3, cache = TRUE)
fit$results
surv_diagnostics(fit)
surv_predict(fit, newdata)
```

Imputation and standardization are learned **inside each analysis split**.
Within that split, cost candidates reuse the prepared design, Hessian and
solver workspace. OSQP also supports warm starts. At most one kernel/solver
workspace is retained, and nothing is shared between folds. Output rows retain
the original candidate/fold ordering. `cache = FALSE` is the cold audit path.
For four costs and three folds, Hessian preparation falls from twelve to three
operations; the winning full-data refit is separate.

For the linear kernel, prediction uses one vector
$w=\sum_{i\in SV}\beta_i x_i$, so a new score is $-(x^\top w+b)$.
This avoids constructing a support-vector by new-observation kernel matrix.
Risk-only output is retained: no survival probability or life expectancy is
attached to the fitted scores.

## What equivalence means

The audit checks the reconstructed Hessian against dense `nearPD`, compares
objective values against an independent dense solver, tests feasibility and
convergence, and compares centered scores, C-indices and tuning selections.
It does **not** assume that matching a C-index proves equal coefficients.

The historical intercept averages residuals over the support set selected
after rounding coefficients to five decimals. Very small solver differences
can change that set and shift every score by a constant. Raw score equality
must therefore be checked separately from equality of ranking. Furthermore,
the historical `quadprog` path can return numerically infeasible coefficients
for ill-conditioned repaired Hessians on the tested system. Such a result is
reported as optimizer failure and cannot win tuning. It is not a valid gold
standard simply because its software call returned successfully.

Only OSQP's full `solved` and Clarabel's full `Solved` statuses are accepted;
Newton uses the independent certificate described above. Iteration limits and
reduced-accuracy external-solver statuses raise errors. Diagnostics retain
the objective, constraint violation, iteration count, primal/dual residuals,
duality gap, support count, solver version and cache use. The feasibility check
uses an absolute threshold `max(1e-5, 100 * tolerance)` on the unrounded dual.

## Limits and reproducible measurements

The reference quadprog path remains dense. Compact additive fits still need
storage for their retained eigenvectors/factors, and can exceed a memory budget
when the required rank is large. No extra modes are dropped to fit that budget.
`memory_limit_mb` is a
workspace **planning estimate**, not a hard runtime cap or measured memory maximum.
Exceeding it raises an error without removing observations. Raising the limit
does not create additional physical RAM.

The accompanying article measures elapsed time and process memory using fresh
R processes. Peak working set includes loaded libraries, whereas fitting time
excludes process startup. Planning estimates and measured peaks describe
different quantities. The application uses dated first-snapshot predictors and
all 23,246 eligible training and 5,812 test drives; 14 source histories lack
positive subsequent-failure follow-up. The replication scripts and measurement
protocol are available in the repository's `paper` directory. Timings apply to
the recorded environment, not every dataset or computing system.
For a sequential additive-kernel example, see
`inst/examples/05_optimized_additive_svm.R` in the package source.

Solver documentation: [OSQP](https://osqp.org/docs/solver/index.html),
[OSQP R interface](https://cran.r-project.org/package=osqp), and
[Clarabel R interface](https://cran.r-project.org/package=clarabel),
[RSpectra](https://cran.r-project.org/package=RSpectra), and
[R Newton minimizer](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/nlm.html).
